title: What Counts as Proof of a Channel

scenes.tts: A hair cell fails when a gene is missing, and the gene's protein sits in the right place. Is that enough to call the protein the channel? A protein can be required for a current without forming the pore. A trafficking factor, an anchor, or a lipid modifying enzyme could all be needed. Deleting any of them would silence the cell.
scenes.visual: Hair cell with a tip link; the current meter empties when the gene is removed; three suspect factors each also explain it

scenes.tts: So the field asks for a ladder of evidence. Each rung rules out a different alternative. The first rung is localization. The protein sits at the lower end of the tip link, where the channel is thought to be. The next rungs are requirement and rescue. In neonatal mouse hair cells lacking both T M C 1 and T M C 2, the conventional current is gone. Put either gene back, and the current returns. That puts the proteins in the pathway. It does not separate a pore from a factor the pore needs.
scenes.visual: Ladder of six rungs builds; meter empties for the double-null, refills with either gene; shows and cannot show lines

scenes.tts: The next rung changes the protein instead. The Beethoven mouse carries one altered residue in T M C 1. In excised neonatal mouse inner hair cells, calcium permeability was reduced. Single channel currents were smaller too. A sequence change that alters which ions pass is strong evidence. A partner can also change permeation, so this rung is strong but not conclusive.
scenes.visual: Channel in a membrane bar passes calcium and other ions; with one residue changed, fewer calcium ions cross; a partner chip could do the same

scenes.tts: The accessibility test starts with cells that already carry current. In mouse hair cells lacking both T M C 1 and T M C 2, Pan and colleagues delivered T M C 1 with a single cysteine substitution. They added a reagent that cannot cross the membrane and reacts with cysteine in water. The reagent changed the permeation of the current. The current existed before the reagent, so altered synthesis or delivery cannot explain the change. The cells still had their native partners.
scenes.visual: Current already flowing; reagent arrives outside, reacts with the engineered cysteine on the channel; flow changes; timeline shows current before reagent

scenes.tts: Purified truncated turtle T M C 1, in liposomes, responded to applied pressure. The proteins were not mammalian, and this was not a native complex. So the answer is a complex of proteins. In mouse cochlear outer hair cells, T M C 1 and T M C 2 did not support transduction without T M I E. Partners such as L H F P L 5 and C I B 2 change what you measure.
scenes.visual: Liposome with channel responds to pressure; then channel chip gathers partner chips TMIE, LHFPL5, CIB2 around it; without TMIE, no transduction

scenes.tts: No single paper climbs every rung. Even a complete ladder says only that the protein forms or lines the pore. It does not say how force from the tip link reaches it. Of each experiment, ask what it ruled out. And ask what it leaves open.
